common_name: Helen Gunning Azalea (White Glenn Dale Hybrid with Tyrian Pink Margins)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Helen Gunning is a Glenn Dale Hybrid bred by B.Y. Morrison with a broad, spreading habit.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade. Helen Gunning is one of the broader-spreading Glenn Dale Hybrid azaleas bred by USDA horticulturist Benjamin Yeo Morrison at the Glenn Dale Plant Introduction Station in Maryland, eventually reaching roughly five feet across on an open, wide-spreading frame rather than the tighter mounds of many Glenn Dale selections. Its flat-faced, ruffled flowers open one to two per cluster in mid-May, with a clean white center set off by margins of deep pinkish-red. Water deeply during dry spells, keep mulch over the shallow root zone, and prune only right after bloom since next year's flower buds set soon afterward.
sources: Journal of the American Rhododendron Society — Studies on Glenn Dale Azaleas at the National Arboretum

common_name: Tama-giku Satsuki Azalea (Variable White-and-Pink Striped Satsuki)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Tama-giku is a traditional Satsuki cultivar whose variable white-and-pink flowers made it a favorite parent among American Satsuki-line breeders.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, mulching to protect the shallow root system through summer heat. Tama-giku is a long-grown Japanese Satsuki azalea whose white flowers are notably unstable in pattern even on a single plant, ranging from nearly pure white to a pale pink wash to bold dark-pink stripes and sectors, a variability that makes every flush slightly different. That same unpredictability made it valuable to hybridizer Robert Gartrell, who paired it with the Gable hybrid 'Louise Gable' as a foundation cross of his Robin Hill azalea breeding program, siring dozens of named Robin Hill cultivars including 'Nancy of Robinhill'. Like other Satsuki selections it flowers later than Kurume or Southern Indica types, typically from late May into June, so prune only in the brief window right after bloom finishes.
sources: Journal of the American Rhododendron Society — Robin Hill Azaleas

common_name: Warai Gishi Satsuki Azalea (Deep Purplish-Pink Satsuki)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Warai Gishi is a classic Satsuki cultivar used by B.Y. Morrison as breeding stock.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, and mulch to keep the shallow roots cool through summer. Warai Gishi is an older Japanese Satsuki cultivar valued for its richly saturated, deep purplish-pink flowers, a strong, uniform color less variable than many patterned Satsuki selections. B.Y. Morrison worked it into his evergreen azalea breeding during the Glenn Dale and Back Acres years, crossing it with 'Vittata Fortunei' to raise the double-flowered hybrids 'Andros' and 'Delos', and the cross 'Kagetsu' x 'Warai Gishi' later produced Morrison's own Back Acres hybrid 'May Blaine' in Mississippi. It blooms later in the season than Kurume or Southern Indica azaleas, typically in late May, so limit pruning to the short window right after flowering ends.
sources: Azalea Society of America — The Azalean, Development of New Satsuki Azalea Hybrids
Journal of the American Rhododendron Society

common_name: Tout a Toi Dahlia (Coral-Rose Decorative Dahlia with Golden Center)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 3-4 inches deep once soil has warmed after the last frost; Tout a Toi is a low, border-height Dutch decorative dahlia later used as a seed parent of the dwarf Gallery series dahlia 'Gallery Renoir' (US Plant Patent PP10,497).

directions: Plant tubers in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil once the ground has warmed. Tout a Toi is a Dutch-raised decorative dahlia bearing coral-rose blooms brightened by a golden center, carried on a notably low, border-friendly plant that stays under two feet tall rather than sprawling like taller decorative types. Breeder Aad Verwer used it as the seed parent, crossed with the dahlia 'Oriental Dream', to raise the compact, painter-named Gallery series introduction 'Gallery Renoir' in 1992 (US Plant Patent PP10,497). Stake lightly only if plants are grown in a windy, exposed site, and lift tubers for winter storage anywhere colder than zone 8.
sources: USPTO Plant Patent PP10,497 — Gallery Renoir Dahlia

common_name: Oriental Dream Dahlia (White Dahlia with Pink-Edged Petals)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep once soil has warmed after the last frost, staking tall stems at planting time; Oriental Dream is a 1990 Dutch dahlia later used as the pollen parent of the Gallery series dahlia 'Gallery Renoir' (US Plant Patent PP10,497).

directions: Plant tubers in full sun in rich, well-drained soil, staking stems early since the flower heads are heavy relative to the foliage. Registered by Dutch breeder Aad Verwer in 1990, Oriental Dream opens white with a thin pink rim around each petal and a soft, buttery-yellow center, the pink margin deepening and spreading further into each petal as the bloom ages — sources differ on whether to classify it as a waterlily or decorative type, but the shifting two-tone effect gives a single planting noticeably different color through its bloom cycle from midsummer into fall. It later served as the pollen parent, crossed with the low decorative dahlia 'Tout a Toi', in raising Aad Verwer's dwarf Gallery series introduction 'Gallery Renoir'. Lift and store tubers over winter anywhere colder than zone 8.
sources: USPTO Plant Patent PP10,497 — Gallery Renoir Dahlia
